q: A nucleoside consists of
c: a nitrogenous base and a five-carbon sugar
a nitrogenous base, a sugar and a phosphate
a nitrogenous base and a phosphate
h: A nucleoTIDE has one more part than a nucleoSIDE.
w: Nucleoside = base + sugar; adding a phosphate makes a nucleotide.

q: Which component is found in RNA but not in DNA?
h: RNA and DNA differ in their sugar and in one of their pyrimidine bases.
w: RNA contains ribose and uracil; DNA contains deoxyribose and thymine. Both have phosphate.

q: A sample of DNA is 20% adenine. What percentage is guanine?
h: A pairs with T and G pairs with C, so A = T and G = C. All four must add to 100%.
w: A = T = 20%, which leaves 100 − 40 = 60% for G + C, so G = 30%. Answering 60% stops before splitting G + C in half; answering 80% subtracts only the adenine (100 − 20) and forgets that thymine also takes 20%.

q: What is the complementary DNA strand for 5′-ACGTTG-3′?
h: Pair A with T and G with C, and remember the two strands are antiparallel.
w: A↔T, C↔G, G↔C, T↔A gives TGCAAC, running in the opposite direction: 3′-TGCAAC-5′. Writing it 5′→3′ with the same letter order ignores the antiparallel arrangement; U appears only in RNA.

q: In the backbone of DNA, nucleotides are linked by
c: phosphodiester bonds joining 3′ and 5′ sugar carbons
hydrogen bonds between bases on the same strand
peptide bonds between neighboring phosphate groups
h: The backbone alternates sugar–phosphate–sugar. What links them?
w: Each phosphate forms ester bonds to the 3′-OH of one sugar and the 5′ carbon of the next: a phosphodiester bond. Hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together, not the backbone.

q: Which base pair is held together by three hydrogen bonds?
h: One of the correct DNA base pairs is held more strongly than the other.
w: G–C forms three hydrogen bonds; A–T (and A–U in RNA) form two. G–T is not a normal base pair.

q: After DNA replication, each new double helix contains
c: one parent strand and one newly made strand
pieces of parent and new DNA mixed in each strand
h: Replication is described as semiconservative. What is conserved?
w: Each parent strand is a template for a new strand, so every daughter helix has one old and one new strand (semiconservative replication).

q: A DNA template strand has the sequence 3′-TACGGC-5′. What is the mRNA transcribed from it?
h: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template, and uses U instead of T.
w: Pairing T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C gives AUGCCG, built 5′→3′: 5′-AUGCCG-3′ (which starts with the start codon AUG). ATG contains T, which RNA does not use.

q: Not counting the stop codon, how many mRNA nucleotides are needed to code for a polypeptide of 50 amino acids?
h: Each codon is a triplet of nucleotides that specifies one amino acid.
w: 50 amino acids × 3 nucleotides per codon = 150 nucleotides. Answering 50 assumes one nucleotide per amino acid; 100 uses two per codon; 17 divides 50 by 3 instead of multiplying.

q: Which mutation is most likely to produce a completely nonfunctional protein?
c: deletion of one base near the start of the gene
substitution of one base in the third position of a codon
substitution that replaces leucine with isoleucine
deletion of three bases (one whole codon) near the end
h: Which change shifts the reading frame of every codon that follows?
w: Deleting one base near the start causes a frameshift, changing every codon after it. Third-position substitutions are often silent, and losing one codon or swapping similar amino acids usually has a smaller effect.

q: A point mutation changes the codon UGG (tryptophan) to UGA (a stop codon). What is the most likely result?
c: The protein is shorter because translation stops early.
Tryptophan is replaced by another amino acid.
The protein is longer than normal.
There is no effect because the codon still starts with UG.
h: What does a stop codon tell the ribosome to do?
w: A new stop codon ends translation early (a nonsense mutation), giving a shortened, usually nonfunctional protein. A swap of one amino acid would be a missense mutation.

q: HIV is a retrovirus. After it infects a cell, which enzyme makes DNA from the virus's RNA genome?
h: This enzyme runs the usual DNA → RNA direction backward.
w: Reverse transcriptase builds DNA using viral RNA as the template. Nucleoside analogs such as AZT block this enzyme. RNA polymerase makes RNA from DNA.

q: Which type of RNA carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome and matches it to a codon on the mRNA?
h: This RNA has an anticodon loop at one end and an amino acid attachment site at the other.
w: tRNA binds its amino acid at the 3′ end and pairs its anticodon with the mRNA codon. mRNA carries the genetic message, rRNA makes up the ribosomes, and snRNA helps remove introns.

q: An mRNA codon is 5′-GCU-3′. What is the anticodon on the tRNA that pairs with it?
h: Pair the bases antiparallel (G–C, A–U). tRNA is RNA, so it uses U, not T.
w: Reading the codon 5′→3′: G pairs with C, C with G, and U with A, giving the antiparallel anticodon 3′-CGA-5′ (the same molecule as 5′-AGC-3′). T is not found in RNA, and 3′-AGC-5′ has the bases in reverse order.

q: A point mutation changes an mRNA codon from CUU to CUC. Both codons code for leucine. What is the effect on the protein?
c: no change, because it is a silent mutation
leucine is replaced by another amino acid
the protein ends early at a stop codon
every amino acid after this point changes
h: Several codons can code for the same amino acid. If the amino acid stays the same, does the protein change?
w: Because the genetic code is redundant, both codons still put leucine into the chain, so the primary structure is unchanged: a silent mutation. Changing every amino acid after the mutation is a frameshift, caused by an insertion or deletion.

q: During DNA replication, the lagging strand is made in short pieces (Okazaki fragments) because
c: DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only in the 5′→3′ direction
DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only in the 3′→5′ direction
helicase unwinds the lagging strand only in short sections
the lagging strand contains uracil, which must be removed
h: The two parent strands are antiparallel, but every new strand must grow in the same chemical direction.
w: DNA polymerase builds new DNA only 5′→3′, adding to a free 3′–OH. The leading strand grows continuously toward the replication fork; the lagging strand must be made in short fragments away from the fork, which DNA ligase then joins.

q: Antibiotics such as tetracycline and streptomycin treat bacterial infections by
c: blocking protein synthesis at bacterial ribosomes
blocking DNA replication inside human cells
destroying the mRNA inside human ribosomes
h: Which step of gene expression (replication, transcription or translation) can a drug block in bacteria alone because bacterial machinery differs from ours?
w: Bacterial ribosomes differ from human ribosomes, so these antibiotics bind bacterial ribosomes and block translation (tetracycline blocks tRNA binding; streptomycin causes misreading of mRNA). Reverse transcriptase inhibitors are antiviral (HIV) drugs.

q: What is the structural difference between ribose and deoxyribose?
c: Deoxyribose has –H instead of –OH on carbon 2′
Deoxyribose has –H instead of –OH on carbon 3′
Deoxyribose has one fewer carbon atom than ribose
Deoxyribose is a six-membered ring; ribose has five atoms
h: “Deoxy” means “missing one oxygen.” Which ring carbon of the sugar carries –H instead of –OH in DNA?
w: Both are five-carbon sugars, but deoxyribose has –H in place of –OH at C2′. The 3′–OH is needed in both to form phosphodiester bonds, so it cannot be the missing one.

q: Which nitrogenous bases are purines, with a double (fused) ring structure?
h: Pyrimidines have a single six-membered ring. A mnemonic: “Pure As Gold.”
w: Adenine and guanine are purines (a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring). C, T and U are single-ring pyrimidines. Each base pair joins one purine with one pyrimidine.

q: In a human cell, where do DNA replication, transcription and translation occur?
c: replication and transcription in the nucleus; translation on ribosomes in the cytoplasm
replication in the nucleus; transcription and translation on ribosomes in the cytoplasm
all three occur on ribosomes attached to the endoplasmic reticulum
replication in the cytoplasm; transcription and translation in the nucleus
h: DNA stays in the nucleus. Which processes need DNA as a template, and where are the ribosomes?
w: Both replication and transcription use DNA as the template, so they happen in the nucleus. The mRNA then leaves through nuclear pores, and translation happens on ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

q: Which DNA replication enzyme is correctly matched with its job?
c: DNA ligase: seals the gaps between DNA fragments
helicase: adds nucleotides to the new strand
DNA polymerase: unwinds the parent double helix
h: Helicase unwinds, primase lays down a short RNA primer, polymerase builds DNA, and one enzyme “glues” pieces together.
w: DNA ligase forms the final phosphodiester bonds that join Okazaki fragments. Helicase breaks the H bonds to unwind the helix, primase makes the RNA primer, and DNA polymerase adds nucleotides 5′→3′.

q: During translation, the anticodon on a tRNA is held to the matching codon on the mRNA by
c: covalent peptide bonds between the bases
phosphodiester bonds between the two strands
ester bonds between the sugars of each RNA
h: Codon–anticodon pairing is temporary, like base pairing in the DNA double helix.
w: The codon and anticodon pair like DNA bases (A–U, G–C), held by hydrogen bonds, so the tRNA can leave after its amino acid is added. Peptide bonds form between amino acids, not between bases.

q: Before translation, each amino acid is attached to its tRNA. What bond joins them in the aminoacyl-tRNA?
c: an ester bond from the amino acid's –COOH to the 3′ end of the tRNA
a peptide bond from the amino acid's –NH<sub>2</sub> to the anticodon
hydrogen bonds between the amino acid's R group and the anticodon
a phosphodiester bond from the amino acid to the 5′ end of the tRNA
h: The 3′ end of every tRNA ends in a sugar with a free –OH. What forms when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol?
w: The amino acid's carboxyl group is joined to the –OH of the ribose at the 3′ end (…CCA) of the tRNA by an ester bond, using ATP. The anticodon is at the other end of the tRNA and pairs with mRNA, not with the amino acid.

q: Which statement about viruses is correct?
c: A virus has DNA or RNA in a protein coat and needs a host cell to reproduce
A virus has both DNA and RNA and its own ribosomes to make proteins
A retrovirus uses reverse transcriptase to make RNA from a DNA template
A virus can make its own proteins outside a cell if it is given amino acids
h: Viruses are not cells. What do they have, and what must they borrow from the cells they infect?
w: A virus is nucleic acid (DNA or RNA, not both) in a protein coat, and it must use the host cell's ribosomes, enzymes and ATP to reproduce. A retrovirus such as HIV makes DNA from its RNA, the reverse of the statement given.

q: In DNA, which base has a single (pyrimidine) ring and pairs with adenine?
h: Pyrimidines have one ring. Adenine's partner differs between DNA and RNA.
w: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine, a pyrimidine, through two hydrogen bonds. Uracil also pairs with adenine but is found in RNA, not DNA; guanine is a purine and cytosine pairs with guanine.

q: In a nucleotide, to which carbons of the pentose sugar are the nitrogenous base and the phosphate group attached?
c: Base at C1′; phosphate at C5′
Base at C5′; phosphate at C1′
Base at C1′; phosphate at C2′
Base at C3′; phosphate at C5′
h: Primed numbers label sugar carbons. The base attaches at the anomeric carbon; the phosphate attaches at the CH<sub>2</sub>–OH carbon outside the ring.
w: The base forms an N-glycosidic bond to C1′, and the phosphate is esterified to the –CH2OH of C5′. The C3′ –OH is used to link to the next nucleotide's phosphate, and C2′ is where ribose and deoxyribose differ.

q: A eukaryotic pre-mRNA contains three exons separated by two introns, with the lengths shown in the table (5′ to 3′). After splicing, how many nucleotides from these regions remain in the mature mRNA?
h: Splicing removes the intervening (noncoding) sequences and joins the expressed sequences together.
w: Introns are cut out and exons are joined: 120 + 85 + 210 = 415 nucleotides. 450 is the total intron length that is removed, and 865 is the unspliced length.

q: Which event occurs during the processing of eukaryotic pre-mRNA in the nucleus?
c: Introns are removed and exons are joined together.
Exons are removed and introns are joined together.
Thymine bases are replaced by uracil bases.
Codons are paired with tRNA anticodons.
h: Processing prepares the transcript before it leaves the nucleus. Which segments carry the code for the protein?
w: Exons are the expressed (coding) regions, so introns are cut out and the exons are spliced together. RNA is made with uracil from the start, and codon–anticodon pairing happens later, during translation on the ribosome.

q: A gene's coding (non-template) DNA strand reads 5′-ATGCCTAG-3′. Which mRNA does RNA polymerase produce from this gene?
h: The mRNA is complementary to the template strand, so it matches the coding strand except for one base.
w: The template strand is 3′-TACGGATC-5′; its complement is the mRNA, which has the same sequence as the coding strand with U in place of T: 5′-AUGCCUAG-3′. Taking the complement of the coding strand gives the template-like sequence 5′-UACGGAUC-3′, the most common mistake.

q: Use this partial genetic code: AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GGC = Gly, CCG = Pro, AAA = Lys, UAA = stop. What peptide is made from the mRNA 5′-AUGUUUGGCUAA-3′?
h: Read the mRNA in groups of three from the 5′ end; a stop codon adds no amino acid.
w: Codons: AUG | UUU | GGC | UAA → Met, Phe, Gly, stop. The peptide is Met–Phe–Gly, written from the N-terminus. Reading 3′ → 5′ gives the reversed order, and UAA codes for no amino acid.

q: Transcription of the template triplet 3′-TAC-5′ gives an mRNA codon. What anticodon must a tRNA carry to recognize that codon?
h: Go two steps: DNA template → mRNA codon (complementary, U for T), then codon → anticodon (complementary and antiparallel).
w: Template 3′-TAC-5′ gives the codon 5′-AUG-3′. The antiparallel anticodon is 3′-UAC-5′ (= 5′-CAU-3′): it has the template's sequence, but with U for T. 5′-UAC-3′ has the right letters with the wrong orientation.

q: Compare the two DNA strands. Original: 5′-GATTACCA-3′. Mutated: 5′-GATACCA-3′. What type of mutation occurred?
h: Count the bases in each strand first.
w: The original has 8 bases and the mutant has 7: one T is missing, so this is a deletion. A substitution would keep the same length with one base changed. A single-base deletion also shifts the reading frame.

q: Which change in the coding region of a gene would NOT cause a frameshift?
h: The mRNA is read three bases at a time. Which change keeps the downstream codons in groups of three?
w: Removing three consecutive nucleotides removes one whole codon (one amino acid), and the reading frame downstream stays the same. Adding or removing 1 or 2 nucleotides shifts every codon after the mutation.

q: During DNA replication, in which direction does DNA polymerase build the new (daughter) strand?
c: 3′ → 5′, adding nucleotides to the 5′ phosphate end
5′ → 3′ on the leading strand but 3′ → 5′ on the lagging strand
Toward and away from each fork at random
h: A new nucleotide's phosphate bonds to a free sugar –OH on the growing chain. Which end has that free –OH?
w: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the free 3′ –OH, so every new strand grows 5′ → 3′. The lagging strand also grows 5′ → 3′; it is made in short Okazaki fragments because it runs away from the fork.

q: Two double-stranded DNA samples have the same length. Sample X is 60% G + C and sample Y is 35% G + C. Which sample needs a higher temperature to separate its two strands, and why?
c: X, because G–C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds
X, because G–C pairs are joined by covalent bonds
Y, because A–T pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds
Y, because more A–T pairs make a longer helix
h: Count hydrogen bonds per base pair for A–T and for G–C.
w: G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs only two, so the G–C-rich sample X has more hydrogen bonds to break. Base pairs between strands are hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.

q: During transcription, RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand. Which base is placed in the RNA opposite each adenine (A) in the template?
h: A pairs with the same partner in RNA as in DNA, but RNA does not contain one of the DNA bases.
w: Adenine pairs with a T/U-type base. RNA has no thymine, so uracil is placed opposite each A. Thymine would be used in DNA replication, not transcription.

q: A forensic lab analyzes a double-stranded DNA sample and finds that 28% of its bases are cytosine. What percentage of the bases are thymine?
h: Base pairing: C pairs with G and A pairs with T, so %C = %G and %A = %T. All four must add to 100%.
w: %G = %C = 28%, so G + C = 56%. A + T = 100% − 56% = 44%, and T is half: 22%. 44% is A and T together, not T alone.

q: A 10-base-pair segment of double-stranded DNA contains 4 G–C pairs and 6 A–T pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands of this segment together?
h: G–C pairs are held by 3 hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs by 2.
w: 4 G–C × 3 = 12 and 6 A–T × 2 = 12, total 24 hydrogen bonds. Swapping the numbers (G–C = 2, A–T = 3) gives 26; using 3 for every pair gives 30; 48 counts each hydrogen bond twice, once from each strand.

q: Hydrolysis of a DNA building block gives guanine, deoxyribose and a single phosphate. What was the building block called?
h: Base + sugar = nucleoside; add phosphates to get a nucleotide. A 'd' marks deoxyribose.
w: Guanine + deoxyribose is the nucleoside deoxyguanosine; one phosphate makes it the nucleotide deoxyguanosine monophosphate (dGMP), a DNA building block. GMP would contain ribose.

q: An mRNA vaccine delivers mRNA for a viral protein into human muscle cells. Which statement describes what happens to that mRNA?
c: It is translated by cytoplasmic ribosomes; the cell's DNA is not changed.
It is copied into DNA by DNA polymerase inside the cell's nucleus.
It is transcribed into a new viral protein inside the cell's nucleus.
It replaces one of the cell's own genes during DNA replication.
h: Transcription (DNA → RNA) happens in the nucleus. Where does translation (mRNA → protein) happen, and which enzyme would be needed to turn RNA into DNA?
w: mRNA is translated by ribosomes in the cytoplasm into protein. Human cells have no reverse transcriptase to copy it into DNA (retroviruses carry that), and DNA polymerase cannot use an RNA template, so the cell's DNA is unchanged.

q: An mRNA has the sequence 5′-AUGGCA-3′. What is the sequence of the DNA template strand from which it was transcribed, written 5′ to 3′?
h: The template strand is complementary and antiparallel to the mRNA, with T instead of U. Write it 3′→5′ under the mRNA, then reverse it.
w: Under 5′-AUGGCA-3′ the template reads 3′-TACCGT-5′; written 5′ to 3′ that is 5′-TGCCAT-3′. 5′-TACCGT-3′ has the right bases in the wrong direction, and 5′-ATGGCA-3′ is the coding strand.

q: Which type of RNA is the most abundant in a cell and combines with proteins to form the ribosome?
h: The name of this RNA comes from the organelle it builds.
w: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) makes up most of the cell's RNA and forms the ribosome together with proteins. mRNA carries the code, and tRNA brings amino acids.

q: The sugar shown is part of a nucleotide. In which nucleic acid is it found, and why?
c: DNA, because C2′ has no –OH (it is deoxyribose)
RNA, because C2′ has no –OH (it is ribose)
DNA, because the ring has five atoms
h: Compare C2′ of the ring: ribose has –OH there; deoxyribose has only H.
w: C2′ carries two H atoms and no –OH, so this is 2-deoxyribose (C5H10O4), the sugar of DNA. Ribose (RNA) is also a five-membered ring with a C3′ –OH; the difference is only at C2′.

q: In the ribose ring shown, which labeled carbon would lose its –OH to make the sugar of DNA?
h: Deoxyribose is "2′-deoxy": the oxygen is missing next to the anomeric carbon.
w: Carbon a is C1′ (anomeric, bonds to the base). Carbon b is C2′; removing its –OH gives 2′-deoxyribose, the DNA sugar. C3′ (c) keeps its –OH to form the phosphodiester bond, and C4′ (d) carries the C5′ CH2OH.

q: The nitrogen base shown is part of ATP. How is it classified?
c: A purine: a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring
A pyrimidine: a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring
A purine: a single six-membered ring
A pyrimidine: a single six-membered ring
h: Purines (A, G) have two fused rings. Pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one ring.
w: This is adenine. It has a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring, the purine ring system (as in guanine). Pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have only one six-membered ring.

q: In double-stranded DNA, which base pairs with the base shown, and how many hydrogen bonds hold the pair together?
h: Identify the base: one ring with an –NH<sub>2</sub> group and one C=O. A pyrimidine always pairs with a purine.
w: The base is cytosine (a pyrimidine with –NH2 and C=O). It pairs with the purine guanine through 3 hydrogen bonds. A–T pairs use 2 hydrogen bonds, which is why G–C-rich DNA is harder to separate.

q: The base shown is found in DNA but not in RNA. Which base pairs with it, and with how many hydrogen bonds?
h: One ring with a –CH<sub>3</sub> group and two C=O groups: which pyrimidine is that?
w: The ring with a methyl group and two C=O groups is thymine. It pairs with adenine through 2 hydrogen bonds. In RNA, uracil (no methyl group) takes thymine's place; uracil does not pair with thymine.

q: An mRNA codon contains the base shown. In standard (Watson–Crick) base pairing, which base on the tRNA anticodon pairs with it?
h: Identify the base (one ring, two C=O, no methyl). In RNA, which purine pairs with it?
w: One ring, two C=O groups and no –CH3: this is uracil, found in RNA in place of thymine. In standard base pairing it pairs with adenine (2 H bonds). Thymine pairs with adenine in DNA; it is not a partner for uracil, and U–U and U–C are not standard pairs.

q: The table shows how each DNA base pairs with a base in DNA and with a base in RNA. Which base fills the blank?
h: RNA has no thymine. Which base takes thymine's place when pairing with adenine?
w: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine; in RNA, thymine is replaced by uracil (U), which also forms two hydrogen bonds with adenine. Choosing T forgets that RNA contains uracil instead of thymine.

q: Translate the mRNA below with the codon table. Which peptide is produced?
h: Read the mRNA 5′→3′ in groups of three, starting at AUG. Translation ends at a stop codon; nothing after it is read.
w: AUG = Met, GCU = Ala, UGG = Trp, then UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends: Met–Ala–Trp. The final GGC (Gly) is never read because it comes after the stop codon. Dropping Met forgets that the start codon also codes for methionine.

q: A single-base substitution in a gene produces the mutated mRNA shown below the original. Using the codon table, what happens to the protein?
c: No change: both codons code for alanine (a silent mutation)
Alanine is replaced by a different amino acid (a missense mutation)
The protein is cut short at the second codon (a nonsense mutation)
Every codon after the change is read in a new frame (a frameshift)
h: Compare the codons one by one. One base changed, but check the table: did the amino acid change?
w: Only the second codon differs: GCU → GCC. The table shows both code for alanine, so the protein is identical: a silent mutation. A substitution keeps the reading frame (no frameshift); a frameshift needs a base inserted or deleted.

q: Two nitrogen bases found in DNA are drawn. Which one is a purine, and which DNA base pairs with it?
h: Purines have two fused rings. Then recall the Watson–Crick pairs: A–T and G–C.
w: Structure I has two fused rings (a six- and a five-membered ring), so it is a purine; its –NH2 and ring pattern make it adenine, which pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds. Structure II is the single-ring pyrimidine cytosine. Pairing I with cytosine confuses adenine with guanine.

q: Structures I–IV are nitrogen bases from nucleic acids. Which one appears only in RNA, never in DNA?
h: Two of these pyrimidines differ by a single methyl group. The one WITHOUT the methyl is the RNA-only base.
w: Structure II is uracil: a pyrimidine with two C=O groups and no methyl group, found only in RNA. Structure I is thymine (uracil plus a –CH3), found only in DNA; III is cytosine and IV is guanine, both present in DNA and RNA.

q: Four nitrogen bases are drawn. Which two are purines?
h: Count the rings: purines have a fused double-ring system; pyrimidines have one six-membered ring.
w: Structures II (adenine) and IV (guanine) each contain two fused rings, the purine skeleton. I (cytosine) and III (thymine) are single-ring pyrimidines. A handy check: in DNA each base pair is one purine plus one pyrimidine (A–T, G–C).

q: The nucleotide shown is a monomer of DNA. Which labeled group is removed when the nucleotide is hydrolyzed to a nucleoside?
h: Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate. Find the phosphate group in the drawing.
w: A nucleoside is just the base joined to the sugar; the nucleotide also carries a phosphate on the 5′ carbon. Removing the phosphate group at a leaves the nucleoside (deoxyadenosine). Position b is on the base, which stays attached to the sugar in a nucleoside.

q: In a DNA strand, the phosphate of the next nucleotide forms a phosphodiester bond with this nucleotide. Which labeled position bonds to that phosphate?
h: The sugar–phosphate backbone links the 5′-phosphate of one nucleotide to a free hydroxyl group on the sugar of the previous one.
w: The backbone of DNA runs 5′ → 3′: the phosphate on the 5′ carbon of the incoming nucleotide bonds to the 3′-hydroxyl group (d) of the growing strand. Position a is this nucleotide's own 5′-phosphate; c is the 2′ carbon, which in DNA has no –OH to bond with.

q: Which labeled position in the nucleotide shown proves that it belongs to DNA rather than RNA?
h: Compare ribose and deoxyribose: the difference is at one specific carbon of the sugar ring.
w: Position c is the 2′ carbon of the sugar, and it carries only hydrogens: no –OH. That makes the sugar 2′-deoxyribose, found only in DNA. Position d is the 3′-OH, present in both DNA and RNA; the phosphate (a) and the base (b) are also common to both.

q: The flow of genetic information in a cell is shown. Which names belong to steps 1 and 2?
h: Transcribing copies the message into the same "language" (nucleic acid); translating changes language (bases → amino acids).
w: Step 1 copies a gene's DNA into mRNA: transcription (DNA → RNA, in the nucleus). Step 2 uses the mRNA codons to build a polypeptide at the ribosome: translation. Replication (DNA → DNA) is not shown in this diagram.

q: The diagram shows the steps from a gene to a protein in a human cell. Which step removes the introns, and where does it happen?
h: Introns are cut out of the first RNA copy before it leaves the nucleus; the trimmed mRNA is what gets translated.
w: Step 1 is transcription, which makes pre-mRNA containing introns and exons. Step 2 is splicing: introns are removed and exons joined, producing mature mRNA; this happens in the nucleus before the mRNA is exported. Step 3 (translation at the ribosome) only reads the already-spliced mRNA.

q: Heating separates the two strands of DNA. The graph shows the percentage of strands separated for samples 1 and 2 as they were warmed. Which sample has the higher G–C content, and why?
c: Sample 2; G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds, so more heat is needed to separate them
Sample 1; A–T pairs have three hydrogen bonds, so more heat is needed to separate them
Sample 1; G–C pairs have two hydrogen bonds, so the strands separate at a lower temperature
Sample 2; G–C pairs are joined by covalent bonds, which break at higher temperature
h: Find which curve needs the higher temperature to reach 50% separated, then recall how many hydrogen bonds each base pair has.
w: Sample 2 reaches 50% separation at about 88 °C versus about 76 °C for sample 1, so sample 2 is harder to pull apart. G–C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds (A–T by only two), so the sample with more G–C pairs, sample 2, has the higher melting temperature. The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.

q: Which class of biomolecule contains phosphodiester linkages in its backbone and nitrogen-containing amines in its monomers?
h: Which polymer has a sugar–phosphate backbone with nitrogen bases hanging off it?
w: In DNA and RNA the phosphate group forms ester bonds to two different sugars (a phosphodiester), and the bases are heterocyclic amines, so nucleic acids fit both clues. Proteins contain amide bonds and amines but no phosphodiesters; triacylglycerols are esters; polysaccharides are acetals.

q: A student made the comparison chart of DNA and RNA shown. One row contains an error. Which one?
h: Check each row against what you know: sugar, bases, number of strands and where each is found.
w: Row III is wrong: RNA contains uracil in place of thymine, so RNA has A, G, C and U, while DNA has A, G, C and T. The other rows are correct: DNA has deoxyribose and RNA has ribose (I), DNA is a double helix and RNA is mostly single-stranded (II), and DNA stays in the nucleus while mRNA travels to ribosomes in the cytoplasm (IV).

q: A liver cell needs the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase, so it first copies that gene into mRNA (transcription). In which part of the cell is this mRNA made?
c: In the nucleus, where the DNA is
In the cytoplasm, on the ribosomes
Outside the nucleus, in the endoplasmic reticulum
h: RNA polymerase must read the DNA template. Where is the cell's DNA kept?
w: In eukaryotic cells the DNA never leaves the nucleus, so RNA polymerase makes mRNA in the nucleus; the finished mRNA is then exported through the nuclear envelope to ribosomes in the cytoplasm, where translation occurs. Replication also happens in the nucleus. A common mix-up is to place transcription with translation in the cytoplasm.

q: During DNA replication, which enzyme unwinds the double helix and separates the two parent strands so they can serve as templates?
h: The name of the enzyme describes its job on the helix.
w: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs and unwinds the helix, forming the replication fork. DNA polymerase then adds complementary nucleotides to each template (5′→3′), DNA ligase seals gaps between fragments, and RNA polymerase is used for transcription, not replication.

q: In translation, a tRNA is attached to its amino acid and also pairs with a codon on the mRNA. Which statement correctly compares the two attachments?
c: The amino acid is held by a covalent ester bond; the codon by hydrogen bonds
The amino acid and the codon are each held by hydrogen bonds between bases
The amino acid is held by hydrogen bonds; the codon by a covalent bond
The amino acid and the codon are each held by covalent peptide bonds
h: Codon–anticodon pairing must be easy to break after the amino acid is delivered. The amino acid must stay firmly attached until then.
w: The amino acid is joined to the 3′ end of its tRNA through a covalent ester bond (aminoacyl-tRNA), while the anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon only through hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (A–U, G–C), which let the tRNA detach once the peptide bond has formed.

q: A DNA template strand segment reads 3′-TAC GGA ATT-5′. Use the codon table given. What peptide is made?
h: Transcribe the template into mRNA (A→U, T→A, C→G, G→C) written 5′→3′, then read codons from the table.
w: Complementary mRNA (5′→3′): AUG CCU UAA. From the table AUG = Met, CCU = Pro and UAA = stop, so translation gives Met–Pro and then stops. "Tyr–Gly–Ile" comes from reading the DNA letters as if they were codons; "Met–Pro–Asn" treats UAA as an amino acid codon; "Asn–Pro–Met" lists the amino acids in the wrong direction (and treats UAA as Asn).
